**Herbert N. Foerstel** (October 6, 1933 – September 20, 2024) was an American librarian and author known for his support of library privacy rights and his research into book banning.

## Early life and education

[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbert_Foerstel&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")

Foerstel was born in St. Louis, Missouri, the second oldest of five children of musicians William Herbert and Margaret Foerstel.<sup about="#mwt6" id="cite_ref-ency_1-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ency&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-ency-1&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-ency-1" id="mwCQ"><span id="mwCg"><span id="mwCw">[</span>1<span id="mwDA">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt9" id="cite_ref-obit2_2-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;obit2&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-obit2-2&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-obit2-2" id="mwDQ"><span id="mwDg"><span id="mwDw">[</span>2<span id="mwEA">]</span></span></a></sup> His parents divorced when he was young and his mother remarried John Boe, a door-to-door encyclopedia salesman who later rose to be a corporate executive. The family moved frequently and Foerstel grew up in Indianapolis, Detroit, Los Angeles, Chicago and Long Island.<sup about="#mwt10" id="cite_ref-obit2_2-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;obit2&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-obit2-2" id="mwEQ"><span id="mwEg"><span id="mwEw">[</span>2<span id="mwFA">]</span></span></a></sup>

He received a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") from [Hamilton College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_College "Hamilton College") in 1955 and an MLS from [Rutgers University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_University "Rutgers University") in 1959. He served in the U.S. Army from 1955 through 1958 working as a radar specialist.<sup about="#mwt13" id="cite_ref-obit_3-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;obit&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-obit-3&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-obit-3" id="mwGQ"><span id="mwGg"><span id="mwGw">[</span>3<span id="mwHA">]</span></span></a></sup> He later earned a master's degree in Science from [Johns Hopkins University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University "Johns Hopkins University") in 1970.

Foerstel started his career as a fine arts librarian from 1959 to 1966 at Towson State University. He then moved to be a science librarian at the [University of Maryland at College Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland,_College_Park "University of Maryland, College Park"), becoming head of the Engineering and Physical Sciences Library. He worked at UMD from 1967 through 1996. He was a member of board of directors of the [National Security Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Archive "National Security Archive") at [George Washington University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_University "George Washington University") and the [Freedom to Read Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_to_Read_Foundation "Freedom to Read Foundation").

While working in libraries, Foerstel wrote a number of books about library censorship and privacy. _Surveillance in the Stacks, The FBI's Library Awareness Program_ was an exposé of the history of the FBI's attempts to infiltrate libraries. Foerstel had met with FBI agents who visited UMD libraries looking for book-lending records of patrons with "Eastern European or Russian-sounding names."<sup about="#mwt16" id="cite_ref-WP_4-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;WP&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-WP-4&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-WP-4" id="mwJg"><span id="mwJw"><span id="mwKA">[</span>4<span id="mwKQ">]</span></span></a></sup> Foerstel did not feel comfortable complying with these requests. He did some research and took part in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit, discovering that the FBI had been visiting science libraries in the United States for 13 years under a project which became known as the [Library Awareness Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_Awareness_Program "Library Awareness Program").<sup about="#mwt19" id="cite_ref-gale_5-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;gale&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-gale-5&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-gale-5" id="mwKw"><span id="mwLA"><span id="mwLQ">[</span>5<span id="mwLg">]</span></span></a></sup> He worked with the university to create and implement policies protecting patron records and later worked with Maryland legislators to advocate for legislation guaranteeing the privacy of all Maryland library records.<sup about="#mwt20" id="cite_ref-obit_3-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;obit&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-obit-3" id="mwLw"><span id="mwMA"><span id="mwMQ">[</span>3<span id="mwMg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt21" id="cite_ref-WP_4-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;WP&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-WP-4" id="mwMw"><span id="mwNA"><span id="mwNQ">[</span>4<span id="mwNg">]</span></span></a></sup> That legislation was passed in 1988. In 1989 Foerstel discovered that as a result of his response to the FBI's inquiries he, himself, was investigated by them.<sup about="#mwt24" id="cite_ref-BS_6-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;BS&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-BS-6&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-BS-6" id="mwNw"><span id="mwOA"><span id="mwOQ">[</span>6<span id="mwOg">]</span></span></a></sup> Foerstel retired from his university work in 1996 and continued to write about First Amendment issues.

_Banned in the U.S.A.: A Reference Guide to Book Censorship in Schools and Public Libraries_ looked at book-banning incidents from 1976 to 1992 and was later updated to include information about book bans, including interviews with authors and reviews of court cases, through 2000.<sup about="#mwt27" id="cite_ref-banned_7-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;banned&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-banned-7&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-banned-7" id="mwPQ"><span id="mwPg"><span id="mwPw">[</span>7<span id="mwQA">]</span></span></a></sup> The book included a Survey of Banned Books which contained annotated entries on the 50 most frequently challenged books from 1996 through 2000.<sup about="#mwt28" id="cite_ref-banned_7-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;banned&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-banned-7" id="mwQQ"><span id="mwQg"><span id="mwQw">[</span>7<span id="mwRA">]</span></span></a></sup> Foerstel was outspoken against crusades to ban books, calling them strongly irrational.<sup about="#mwt31" id="cite_ref-stl_8-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;stl&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-stl-8&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-stl-8" id="mwRQ"><span id="mwRg"><span id="mwRw">[</span>8<span id="mwSA">]</span></span></a></sup>

## Personal life and death

[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbert_Foerstel&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life and death")

Foerstal married Lenora Shargo, an art professor who he met while they were carpooling from their shared apartment building to Towson.<sup about="#mwt32" id="cite_ref-obit_3-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;obit&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-obit-3" id="mwSw"><span id="mwTA"><span id="mwTQ">[</span>3<span id="mwTg">]</span></span></a></sup> The couple had three children.<sup about="#mwt33" id="cite_ref-obit_3-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;obit&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-obit-3" id="mwTw"><span id="mwUA"><span id="mwUQ">[</span>3<span id="mwUg">]</span></span></a></sup> Lenora died in 2018. Herbert Foerstel died on September 20, 2024, at the age of 90.<sup about="#mwt34" id="cite_ref-obit2_2-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;obit2&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-obit2-2" id="mwUw"><span id="mwVA"><span id="mwVQ">[</span>2<span id="mwVg">]</span></span></a></sup>

Foerstal won a [Hugh Hefner First Amendment Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_M._Hefner_First_Amendment_Award "Hugh M. Hefner First Amendment Award") in 1988. His 1991 book _Surveillance in the Stacks_ was chosen by [Choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choice_(publisher) "Choice (publisher)") as a Best Academic Book in 1990.<sup about="#mwt35" id="cite_ref-ency_1-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ency&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Foerstel#cite_note-ency-1" id="mwXA"><span id="mwXQ"><span id="mwXg">[</span>1<span id="mwXw">]</span></span></a></sup>
